title: Agent Authorization Explained
summary: Authorization is not one decision but several, checked in sequence. A plain walkthrough of the layers, the intersection rule, and why the two most common failures sit at opposite extremes.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Authorization is not one decision. It's several, checked in sequence, and most agent incidents trace back to only one of them ever being checked.** A team wires up a login, confirms the agent is who it says it is, and calls that "authorized" — but identity only answers who is acting, not what they're allowed to do.


The common shortcut treats authentication as a stand-in for authorization: verify the agent, assume the rest is fine. That's backwards. A perfectly identified agent with no limit on its reach is exactly as dangerous as an anonymous one, because identity tells you who broke something, not whether they were allowed to.


None of this means locking agents down until they're useless. The opposite failure is just as common and a lot harder to notice: an agent that quietly inherits everything the person it serves can do, looking fine right up until the day it actually uses that inherited reach.


What holds up is layered: a request clears identity, then who it's acting for, then which tool, then which action, then which data, before it runs at all. Any single layer can deny it.


Design the layers before you design the login screen.


## Overview


An agent that only answers questions is limited by what it can say. An agent that can act, retrieving records, calling tools, updating systems, sending messages, is limited by what it's allowed to do, and that limit is what authorization defines.


Most teams building their first agent get identity right and stop there. The agent has a service account, it authenticates cleanly, the logs show exactly which agent connected to which system. That feels like the hard part is done. We don't think it is: knowing precisely which agent reached the data warehouse doesn't help if that agent was free to export every table in it once it got there.


This post separates authorization from the identity question it usually gets bundled with, then walks through why agents make it harder than it is for a person, the layered model that keeps it under control, and how it connects to the record of what actually happened.


**A system that can only say who acted, and not how far they were allowed to reach, is only half built.**


## Two Questions, Not One


Authentication and authorization get treated as one step because they usually happen in the same login flow. They aren't the same question, and they don't fail the same way.


Authentication answers *who or what is this agent* . It establishes identity. Authorization answers *what is this agent allowed to do* . It establishes boundaries. A system can nail the first and completely skip the second, and from the outside it looks fine right up until the agent does something nobody meant to allow.


## Why It's Hard for Agents


Authorization for people is a settled discipline: roles, groups, access reviews. Agents complicate it because they sit between a person and a system, and they act continuously, at machine speed, usually on someone else's behalf.


The trap is inheritance. An agent acting for a user is not the user, and shouldn't quietly absorb everything that user is allowed to do. A finance analyst can post journal entries; their reconciliation agent might read balances and propose an adjustment, never post one. A recruiter can send offer letters; their sourcing agent can draft outreach, not send it to a real inbox unsupervised. A data engineer can query production directly; their analytics agent gets a read replica with sensitive fields stripped out. In every case the human has more authority than the agent working in their name, on purpose. An agent is faster and less context-aware than the person it serves, so its grant should be narrower than theirs, not equal to it.


## The Intersection Rule


The safer way to reason about this: an action is allowed only when both the user and the agent are separately permitted to take it. Not one or the other. Both.


```text
allow(action) = permitted_for(user) AND permitted_for(agent)


# Procurement example
user (buyer):  can create POs, can approve POs up to $250k
agent:         can create POs, cannot approve any PO


create_po($40k)   -> user: yes,  agent: yes   -> ALLOWED
approve_po($40k)  -> user: yes,  agent: no    -> BLOCKED, needs a person
```


This fails closed by design. A marketing operations agent might be technically capable of publishing a campaign, and the marketer might personally have publish rights, but if the agent's own grant stops at drafting, the campaign waits for a person regardless of what its user is allowed to do. The user's broad authority never leaks into the agent, because the agent's own grant is the one being checked.


## The Layers


A single allow-or-deny flag is too coarse for something that chains tools together. A request has to clear several checks, each one narrower than the last.


**Figure 1 — A request has to clear every layer before it runs. One denial anywhere in the chain stops it.**


Walking the layers in order: **agent identity** confirms this is a recognized, governed agent rather than a borrowed credential. **User context** establishes who it's acting for right now, since the same agent serving a junior rep and a team lead may resolve to different limits. **Tool access** decides which systems it can reach at all, a legal review agent might connect to the contract repository and never to payments. **Action permissions** narrow that further: reaching the ticketing system is not the same as being allowed to close, reassign, or delete a ticket in it. **Data boundaries** scope which records it can see, an IT agent confined to one region's servers, an HR agent to one department. **Conditions** restrict a permission to specific circumstances: a time window, a transaction size, an active incident. And some actions need a person regardless of everything else checking out, the last layer, which stops the request rather than approving it automatically.


We think the layer people skip most often is conditions, because it's the one that requires thinking about *when* a permission should hold rather than just *what* it covers, and that question rarely comes up until an agent uses a legitimate grant at an illegitimate moment.


## Least Privilege Is the Default


The principle matters more for agents than for almost any human role: give an agent only the minimum it needs, nothing held "just in case."


Broad access is a quiet temptation during development, because granting full admin removes friction while you iterate. That convenience turns into risk the moment the agent reaches production and starts operating unattended, at scale. An over-permissioned agent doesn't just have more capability sitting unused; it has a wider blast radius the moment a prompt gets manipulated, a tool misbehaves, or the model reasons its way into something nobody intended. Start narrow, observe what the agent genuinely needs, and widen only when a real task demands it. Access that's easy to grant should be just as easy to pull back.


## Authorization Without a Record Is Half a Control


Knowing what an agent was allowed to do is only half of it. You also need to know what it actually did, and whether the two matched.


Every consequential decision the authorization layer makes, what was requested, which permission applied, whether it was allowed, blocked, or held for a person, belongs in the record next to the action itself. When a sales agent updates a forecast, the record should connect the action to the agent's identity, who it was acting for, the permission that applied, and the outcome. Without that link, authorization is a claim about how the system is supposed to work. With it, you can answer the question that actually comes up in an incident: what was allowed, and did anything happen outside the lines.


## In Practice


Teams that get this right share a habit: they write down what an agent may *do* , not just what it may *reach* . "Can call the HR system" isn't a permission. "Can read leave balances, cannot edit them" is.


They also draw a hard line between the reversible and the irreversible. Drafting, proposing, simulating: let those run freely. Sending, posting, merging, deleting, paying: those sit behind a tighter scope or a person, every time. And they keep the agent's identity distinct from the user's, so the intersection rule stays real rather than becoming a formality nobody actually checks. Grants get reviewed on a schedule, because access accumulated for a one-off task rarely gets removed on its own.


None of this is bureaucracy for its own sake. We think it's what lets a team put a hundredth agent into production without renegotiating trust from scratch each time.


## The Boundary That Makes Autonomy Usable


Good authorization makes agents safer and easier to scale at the same time. It gives builders a clear line to work within and gives security teams a real answer, not a hope, for whether an agent can act outside its approved limits.


Once you know who the agent is, the real work is deciding what it can do with that identity: layers that compose, an intersection rule that keeps a user's authority from leaking into the agent, least privilege as the starting point rather than an afterthought, and a record that proves the boundary held.


**Authorization is the line between useful automation and autonomy nobody actually decided to grant. Skip it and the question isn't whether an agent oversteps — it's when.**
